## What is a Bloom filter? {background-image="figures/static/bloom1970.png" background-size="contain" background-position="right" background-opacity="0.18"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}

A space-efficient, probabilistic data structure that answers:

> **Is $x$ in the set?**

- **"Definitely not"**, or **"probably yes"**
- False positives are possible; false negatives are not
- Trades a small error rate for a lot of memory

::: {.small}
Burton H. Bloom, *Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors*,
Communications of the ACM 13(7), July 1970
:::

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- Bloom worked at Computer Usage Company, Newton Upper Falls, Massachusetts.
- His motivating example: automatic hyphenation of a 500,000-word dictionary.
  About 90% of words follow simple rules; the other 10% need an expensive
  disk lookup for their hyphenation pattern.
- The filter sits in core memory and holds the 10% "hard" words. If it says
  "definitely not", hyphenate by rule; if "probably yes", go to disk.
- A false positive only costs an unnecessary disk read, never a wrong answer.
- His result: a hash area 18% of the size of an error-free hash table still
  eliminates 87% of the disk accesses.
- He called false positives "errors of commission".
:::
